panels.rationale: Single H&E histopathology image from a patient case/article focused on Stevens–Johnson syndrome, showing the captioned characteristic full-thickness epidermal necrosis. [raw subtype: stevens_johnson_syndrome]
panels.attribution_text: Frantz et al. Stevens-Johnson Syndrome and Toxic Epidermal Necrolysis: A Review of Diagnosis and Management.. Medicina (Kaunas, Lithuania) 2021. doi:10.3390/medicina57090895. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 2.
panels.figure_caption: Histopathology of Stevens–Johnson Syndrome. Full thickness epidermal necrosis, an orthokeratotic stratum corneum, and sparse dermal inflammation are typical and supportive but nonspecific features.
in_text_mentions: cludes other desquamating and vesiculobullous dermatoses, such as pemphigus vulgaris, linear IgA bullous dermatosis, staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome (SSSS), and erythema multiforme major (EMM). Importantly, EMM and SJS/TEN were historically classified as existing on the same disease spectrum, as the clinical and histopathologic presentation (Figure 2) of these diseases can be similar, but were later determined to be distinct diseases [6,13,14,15,16]. Thus, the diagnosis must be made on clinical parameters. Key features of these disorders are outlined in Table 4 [1,6,13,14,15,16,43,44,45].
